Balanced Bagging for Extreme Class Imbalance

PLS-DA Classification of Simulated NIR Spectra with ~100:1 Class Ratio
Technical Report — Dual Bootstrap (Subsample Majority + Oversample Minority)

Executive Summary

0.000
Defective F1 — without Bootstrap
1.000
Defective F1 — with Balanced Bagging

This report demonstrates how balanced bagging (dual bootstrapping) rescues PLS-DA classification performance under extreme class imbalance. We simulate 10,000 NIR spectra with a 99:1 ratio between Normal (9,900) and Defective (100) samples — mimicking real-world scenarios such as fraud detection, rare-defect screening, and medical diagnosis.

Without resampling, PLS-DA trained on this skewed data produces a degenerate model that predicts every sample as Normal, achieving 50% accuracy on a balanced prediction set and completely failing the Defective class (F1 = 0). With balanced bagging — where each of 100 ensemble rounds trains on a balanced subset created by subsampling the majority and oversampling the minority via bootstrap — the model recovers perfect classification (F1 = 1.000 for both classes).

Key Result: Balanced bagging improved Macro-F1 from 0.333 to 1.000 (+0.667) and overall accuracy from 50% to 100% on the held-out balanced prediction set, while the underlying AUC remained at 1.000 for both models — proving that the spectral signal was always present but the imbalanced training regime prevented the standard model from exploiting it.

Background & Motivation

Class imbalance is pervasive in real-world classification tasks. In NIR spectroscopy for quality control, a production line might generate thousands of normal samples for every defective one. In fraud detection, legitimate transactions outnumber fraudulent ones by 100:1 or more. Standard classifiers trained on such data learn to predict the majority class for every sample — achieving high overall accuracy while completely failing the class we actually care about detecting.

Partial Least Squares Discriminant Analysis (PLS-DA) is the workhorse classifier in chemometrics. It performs well when classes are balanced, but its underlying regression mechanism (plsregress) is particularly vulnerable to imbalance: the regression line is pulled toward the mean of Y, and when Y ≈ 0.01 (99% zeros), the predicted values for both classes cluster near zero — well below any reasonable decision threshold.

Why Balanced Bagging?

The solution is balanced bagging (also called EasyEnsemble or Balanced Random Forest), a dual bootstrap strategy. In each of B rounds, we (a) bootstrap-subsample the majority class down to nbal samples, (b) bootstrap-oversample the minority class up to nbal samples, and (c) train PLS-DA on this balanced subset. The final prediction is the average of all B soft votes. This approach has three advantages over simple oversampling: majority subsampling creates diverse training sets across rounds; minority oversampling with replacement generates variation; and soft-vote averaging produces a robust, low-variance ensemble.

Pipeline Overview

Step 1 — Simulated NIR Data & Class Imbalance

We simulate 10,000 NIR spectra across 256 wavelength bands (400–2,500 nm). The majority class (Normal, class 0) contains 9,900 samples (99%) and the minority class (Defective, class 1) contains 100 samples (1%), giving a 99:1 imbalance ratio. This is representative of real-world rare-event detection scenarios.

The Defective class carries a subtle multi-band spectral signature: a +0.045 bump at 1730 nm (C-H 1st overtone), a −0.030 dip at 1450 nm (O-H combination), and a +0.025 bump at 2100 nm (C-H combination). Realistic noise sources include per-wavelength Gaussian noise (σ = 0.030), sample-to-sample baseline tilt, offset variation, and multiplicative scatter simulating particle-size and path-length effects.

Figure 1a: Left — Raw NIR spectra (blue = Normal, orange = Defective) with Normal class brought forward, plus the extreme 9900:100 class distribution. Right — Preprocessed spectra after SNV and Savitzky-Golay 1st derivative.
Figure 1b: Same data with Defective class brought forward using the interactive toggle. The Defective mean (orange) shows subtle but systematic differences from the Normal mean (blue), particularly visible in the SG derivative near 1450 and 1730 nm.

Step 2 — Spectral Preprocessing

Two standard preprocessing methods are applied sequentially:

Standard Normal Variate (SNV) removes additive baseline offset and multiplicative scatter by centering and scaling each spectrum individually. Savitzky-Golay 1st derivative (window = 15, polynomial order = 2) eliminates any residual baseline and enhances spectral features by converting broad absorption bands into sharper derivative peaks. The combination is standard practice in NIR chemometrics and improves PLS-DA performance by removing non-chemical variation.

Preprocessing Note: SNV and SG derivative are applied before any resampling, so the correction statistics (mean, std) are computed on the original sample. This prevents the bootstrap resampling from distorting the spectral preprocessing.

Step 3 — Training / Prediction Set Split

A balanced prediction set (Pset) is constructed by randomly drawing 30 samples from each class (60 total). This balanced Pset ensures that plain accuracy gives equal weight to both classes — accuracy on a balanced set equals balanced accuracy. All remaining samples form the Training set (Tset): 9,870 Normal + 70 Defective, an even more extreme 141:1 ratio.

Figure 2: Training set (left) retains the extreme imbalance (9870 vs 70), while the prediction set (right) is deliberately balanced (30 vs 30) for fair evaluation.

Step 4 — Balanced Bagging (Dual Bootstrap)

This is the core methodological contribution. Unlike simple minority oversampling (which matches the minority count to the full majority), balanced bagging applies bootstrap resampling to both classes simultaneously:

Algorithm — Balanced Bagging (B=100, nbal=300):
For each round b = 1, …, 100:
 (a) Draw 300 samples with replacement from 9,870 majority → subsample majority
 (b) Draw 300 samples with replacement from 70 minority → oversample minority
 (c) Train PLS-DA on the balanced 600-sample set
 (d) Predict Pset → store soft probabilities
Final prediction = mean of 100 probability vectors, threshold at 0.5.

Each round uses only 3% of the majority samples (300/9,870), but across 100 rounds the ensemble covers approximately 95% of all majority samples. The minority’s 70 unique spectra are drawn repeatedly with different random combinations, providing diversity without generating synthetic samples (unlike SMOTE, which can produce unrealistic spectra in high-dimensional space).

Figure 3: Balanced bagging overview. From left: original Tset (141:1), a single balanced round (300 vs 300), majority coverage across 50 rounds (most samples drawn 1–5 times), and the bootstrap vote distribution showing clean class separation.

Step 5 — PLS Score Plots & 3D Density

PLS score plots project the high-dimensional spectral data onto the first two latent variables (LVs) — the directions of maximum covariance with the class label Y.

Figure 4: 2D PLS score plots. Left (woBS): 9,870 majority samples form a dense cloud with 70 minority samples clustered separately — the classes are separable but the imbalanced PLS model cannot exploit it. Right (wBS, 1 round): balanced 300 vs 300 training set shows clear two-cluster structure.
Figure 5: 3D histograms (z = sample count per bin). Left: the majority class forms a towering mountain (peak >400 samples/bin) while the minority is a barely visible bump at its base — viscerally demonstrating the density imbalance. Right: after balanced bagging, both classes have comparable heights (∼10–15 per bin).

Step 6 — Predicted-Y Distributions (Key Diagnostic)

This is the most diagnostic visualisation. PLS-DA predicts a continuous Ŷ value for each sample; the 0.5 threshold converts it to a class label.

Figure 6: Predicted-Y distributions on the balanced Pset. Left (woBS): both classes cluster between 0 and 0.2 — far below the 0.5 threshold — so everything is classified as Normal. Right (wBS): clean bimodal separation with Normal near 0 and Defective near 1.
Why does this happen? PLS regression minimises the squared error between Xβ and Y. When 99% of Y = 0, the intercept alone (≈ 0.01) already explains most variance. The regression coefficient β is scaled down proportionally, compressing all predictions toward ~0.01. Balanced bagging recentres the training Y to mean = 0.5, giving the regression full dynamic range to separate the classes.

Step 7 — Variable Importance

Figure 7: Left: PLS-DA regression coefficients. The imbalanced model (blue) has near-zero coefficients — it essentially does not use the spectral information. The balanced model (green) shows large, structured coefficients at the signature wavelengths (1450, 1730, 2100 nm). Right: Variable Importance in Projection (VIP) scores confirm the same three wavelength regions.

The regression coefficient comparison is striking: without balancing, the PLS-DA model’s coefficients are so compressed that the spectral features are effectively invisible. The balanced model amplifies these coefficients by orders of magnitude, correctly identifying the discriminative wavelength regions. The VIP plot independently confirms that wavelengths near 1450, 1730, and 2100 nm — exactly where the simulated defect signature was injected — are the most important variables.

Step 8 — Confusion Matrices

Figure 8: Confusion matrices on the balanced Pset (30+30). Left (woBS): all 60 samples are predicted as Normal — 30 correct (TN), 30 missed defectives (FN). Right (wBS): perfect 30/30 classification for both classes.

Final Results & Performance Comparison

Metric Without Bootstrap (woBS) With Balanced Bagging (wBS) Improvement (Δ)
Accuracy 0.500 1.000 +0.500
Class 0 (Normal) F1 0.667 1.000 +0.333
Class 1 (Defective) F1 0.000 1.000 +1.000
Macro-F1 0.333 1.000 +0.667
AUC (ROC) 1.000 1.000 +0.000
Target achieved: With balanced bagging, both classes achieve F1 = 1.000 (> 90% target). Without balancing, Class 0 F1 = 0.667 and Class 1 F1 = 0.000 — both significantly worse than the balanced model, with the Defective class showing catastrophic failure as intended.
Figure 9: ROC curves and summary performance dashboard. Both models achieve AUC = 1.0 (the signal is intrinsically separable), but only the balanced bagging model can exploit this at the 0.5 decision threshold.

Discussion

1. AUC Paradox: Perfect AUC, Zero F1

Perhaps the most interesting finding is that both models achieve AUC = 1.000, yet the imbalanced model has F1 = 0 for the Defective class. This illustrates a well-known but often overlooked point: AUC measures discriminability across all possible thresholds, while F1 depends on a specific threshold (0.5). The imbalanced model’s predicted values are perfectly rank-ordered (all Defective samples score higher than all Normal samples), but the absolute values are so compressed (all below 0.2) that the standard 0.5 cutoff fails. One could recover performance by optimising the threshold — but in practice, balanced bagging is more principled because it fixes the root cause (biased regression) rather than patching the symptom (wrong threshold).

2. Why Dual Bootstrap Beats Simple Oversampling

In the earlier iterations of this project, simple minority oversampling (inflating 70 minority samples to match 9,870 majority) was used. This has two problems: (a) training on 9,870 + 9,870 = 19,740 samples is computationally expensive per round, and (b) the minority class is repeated ~141 times each, leading to severe memorisation. Dual bootstrapping with nbal = 300 trains on just 600 samples per round — 33× faster — while the ensemble of B = 100 rounds still covers most majority samples and generates diverse minority subsets.

3. Analogy to Fraud Detection

The 99:1 ratio in this demo mirrors real-world fraud detection, where legitimate transactions vastly outnumber fraudulent ones. In both domains, the cost of missing a positive (undetected fraud, undetected defect) far exceeds the cost of a false alarm. Balanced bagging is widely used in the fraud detection industry precisely because it handles extreme imbalance without requiring synthetic data generation, making it suitable for domains where the feature space is complex and interpolation-based methods (SMOTE) may produce unrealistic samples.

4. Regression Coefficient Amplification

The regression coefficient comparison (Figure 7) provides a mechanistic explanation for why balancing works. In the imbalanced model, the PLS regression coefficients are compressed to near-zero because the regression target Y has almost no variance (99% zeros). After balancing, Y has equal variance in both directions, and the regression is free to assign large, meaningful coefficients to the wavelengths that actually discriminate between classes. This is not just a threshold issue — the model genuinely learns different spectral features.

5. Practical Considerations

The choice of nbal = 300 and B = 100 is not deeply optimised. In practice, nbal should be large enough that each balanced subset captures sufficient spectral variation (typically 100–500 per class), and B should be large enough for stable averaging (50–200 is typical). The number of PLS latent variables was selected by 5-fold stratified cross-validation on a balanced subsample, independently of the imbalanced model’s LV selection.

Conclusion

This demonstration confirms that balanced bagging (dual bootstrap) is a powerful, practical solution for PLS-DA classification under extreme class imbalance. The key takeaways are:

1. Standard PLS-DA catastrophically fails at 99:1 imbalance — predicting every sample as the majority class, with Defective F1 = 0.

2. Balanced bagging recovers perfect classification (F1 = 1.000 for both classes) by training an ensemble of B = 100 models on balanced subsets.

3. The spectral signal was always present (AUC = 1.000 for both models) — imbalance doesn’t destroy information, it prevents the model from exploiting it.

4. Dual bootstrapping (subsample majority + oversample minority) is faster and more diverse than simple oversampling, and avoids the pitfalls of synthetic sample generation in high-dimensional spectral data.

5. The approach is directly applicable to real-world rare-event detection: fraud screening, defect identification, medical diagnosis, and any NIR spectral classification with highly imbalanced classes.
